Bien que le hip-hop soit l’un des genres: Although hip-hop is one of the most-streamed music genres in Quebec, it remains underrepresented in mainstream media. Filling a gap, Le WarmUp FM gives visibility and a platform to artists whose success is undeniable, but who remain in the shadows, far from the spotlight.
Comme chaque jeudi, Antony et Freddy s’i: Like every Thursday, Antony and Freddy settle comfortably in front of their mics. Across from them, comedian Oussama Fares is stopping by their weekly radio show.
Il parlera de lui et de ses projets, ava: He’ll talk about himself and his projects before giving up his seat to rapper White Migz, who has come with his crew to perform live.
Une autre semaine qui se conclut pour Le: Another week wraps up for Le WarmUp, one of the few radio shows focused on Montréal’s hip-hop scene. Since starting out in 2018, the two hosts have made it their mission to hand the mic to artists who are popular in the community but often ignored by the major media.
Bien que l’émission du WarmUp FM soit pr: Although Le WarmUp FM airs on a community station, Radio Centre-Ville 102.3 FM, it quickly made its mark in the scene, with some of the most-streamed artists in the city, including Izzy-S, Tizzo and Raccoon, making appearances.
« Tous les médias qui se présentent cont: “All the media that compete with us show something else. We put forward what the big media don’t want to show. I think the artists appreciate that and feel at home when they come here,” says Freddy Lloyd, one of Le WarmUp’s two hosts.
« C’est important que le monde réalise q: “It’s important for people to realize it’s been a lot of investment since the beginning. We haven’t made money off the show. We do it for the culture,” adds Antony Dagger, the show’s founder, sitting beside him.
L’émission a grandi à un point tel que c: The show has grown to the point that some people are willing to pay to be invited. Its credibility allows the two hosts to attract some of the biggest names on the local scene.
« On ne veut pas que notre show devienne: “We don’t want our show to become a place where you can pay to come on. Otherwise, it has no value, anybody could come,” Freddy cautions, however. Live performances are also part of the show’s format. The space next to the studio can hold up to a hundred people, giving artists the chance to perform in front of an audience. “Coming is one thing, but once you see how it’s presented, it’s ultra-professional. And the comfort they have here, they won’t get anywhere else,” Freddy adds.
L’automne dernier, par exemple, le rappe: Last fall, for example, rapper Shreez was on site with his crew to launch his album Je suis canicule. “They play our music and give us a platform. It’s a way of giving back,” the rapper explains over the phone. He had discovered the show through Instagram himself and made a few appearances over time, before agreeing to hold his launch there.
« Ça montre que tu peux faire confiance: “It shows that you can trust the artists. They’re professionals who just want to share their music. Maybe at Radio-Canada, they wouldn’t feel as comfortable. With us, there’s no barrier. We grow together,” Antony Dagger emphasizes.
« C’est presque la même chose que La sem: “It’s almost the same thing as La semaine des 4 Julie or Belle et Bum, except it’s hip-hop. It’s something you don’t get anywhere else in Montréal – the artist can come, people listen to them in the room and we put on a live show,” says Freddy Lloyd, drawing the comparison.
Raccoon, de son vrai nom Shamyr Daléus-L: Raccoon, whose real name is Shamyr Daléus-Louis, has appeared on Le WarmUp a few times. For him, the show stands out for its content, which mixes freestyles and interviews, while also debuting new tracks as exclusives.
« Les médias traditionnels sont un peu f: “Traditional media are a bit wary of hip-hop. To have a hip-hop outlet, you already have to be a connoisseur or a fan of the culture to be able to do a good interview and understand what’s going on,” he says. “It’s a show that gives so much to the culture! They’re pioneers. These are guys who were there before this urban buzz or this whole diversity thing and all that. We’ve been watching them grind for a long time. When I get the chance, I’m happy to come here,” says comedian Oussama Fares, who discovered the show online.

Le WarmUp est plutôt unique dans le pays: Le WarmUp is fairly unique in Quebec’s media landscape. Although Montréal hip-hop artists can each rack up hundreds of thousands of streams on online platforms, they are very often sidelined by the major media.
« Le gros problème pour moi, c’est que l: “The big problem for me is that hip-hop culture has codes that the major media don’t know. That’s where it becomes a problem and there’s a split between the two. In the United States, that’s less the case. Hip-hop culture is more a part of popular culture,” explains Félix B. Desfossés. A journalist specializing in the history of music in Quebec, he is the author of the book Les racines du hip-hop au Québec, among others.
Depuis quelques années, il remarque cepe: In recent years, however, he has noticed the door opening wider, with artists like Koriass and Souldia managing to secure a place in traditional media. It is a place that is harder to claim, though, for artists from diverse backgrounds.
« Je ne pense pas que ce soit volontaire: “I don’t think it’s intentional on the part of the major media, but I believe there’s something that reflects Quebec society and its problem with systemic racism. I see something unintentional in these media, like telling themselves that certain faces will appeal more to the general public,” Desfossés laments.
Une situation d’autant plus ironique que: The situation is all the more ironic given that many of these artists get more streams online than some of Quebec’s media stars. For example, for the period from October 15 to December 30, 2021, Enima was the most-streamed Quebec performer on online platforms, according to a report by the Observatoire de la culture et des communications du Québec.
« Les grands médias ne comprennent pas q: “The major media don’t understand that they could be building the audience of the future if they went to the artists with the big numbers,” Desfossés points out.
Il croit néanmoins qu’il est possible, p: He nevertheless believes it is possible for a racialized artist to become a star in Quebec, provided they tick “certain ‘mainstream’ boxes.” He points to the group Muzion, which in his view managed to do so without compromising its artistic integrity.
« Il ne faut pas oublier que les station: “We can’t forget that the radio stations here are pop music stations. Some lyrics aren’t accepted at the pop level in Quebec. But like I tell artists, today they don’t need radio to promote themselves anymore,” notes Malik Shaheed, referring to the democratization of the internet and the arrival of social media.
Il estime également que les artistes doi: He also believes artists need to find ways to broaden their audience in francophone markets outside Quebec. A former VJ at MusiquePlus, he hosted a hip-hop show there, among other things. He has also worked at various radio stations over the years.
« Pour les artistes, c’était leur seule: “For the artists, that was their only visibility; the radio stations didn’t want to know anything about it,” he recalls, referring to his years at MusiquePlus. And although he had the support of his director, he had only one hour a week to play the latest videos, from Quebec as well as the United States and France.
« Il y a encore de la résistance contre: “There’s still resistance to hip-hop, and the artists who get played on the radio aren’t the Black artists. But the people who started hip-hop were Black, just like the ones who keep it moving. But that’s not the image being put out today,” Shaheed laments.
Selon lui, la situation ne changera pas: According to him, the situation won’t change until there are people “who look like the artists” within the major media. “[Otherwise], you’ll always have the problem, because they don’t understand the message and the culture,” he says, noting in passing the need for “white allies” to move things forward.

Freddy Lloyd a grandi à Montréal dans le: Freddy Lloyd grew up in Montréal’s Côte-des-Neiges neighbourhood in a family of Haitian origin. It was through his family and the people around him that he discovered hip-hop music at a very young age.
« J’ai étudié en communication, et les m: “I studied communications, and I’ve always been interested in media. I always found it strange that we didn’t have a hip-hop outlet on the radio. I was looking for the chance to do what we’re doing now,” he says.
De son côté, Antony Dagger, l’autre anim: For his part, Antony Dagger, the show’s other host, lived in Montréal’s east end before moving to Laval. It was at Collège de Bois-de-Boulogne that his interest in the media world was confirmed.
« J’ai fait communication-cinéma, mais j: “I did communications and film, but I spent more time at the campus radio station than in my classes,” he recalls. “From the start, I loved it, I loved putting myself out there. I really stood out there, and that’s what led me to become who I am today.”
Il a travaillé à une première émission,: He worked on a first show, Le WarmUp du Week-end, which eventually formed the backbone of Le WarmUp FM.
« C’était un peu comme un bébé qui se fo: “It was kind of like a baby taking shape, but I didn’t have the right team to do it. And then my cousin introduced me to Freddy and we connected,” he explains.
C’était à l’été 2018. La chimie s’est ra: That was in the summer of 2018. The chemistry between them was quick to set in. This coming October, the two partners will celebrate their show’s fifth anniversary.
« Tous les deux, on cherchait à couvrir: “We were both looking to cover the urban scene. I’d often talked to Antony about how I thought there was room for a hip-hop radio station or show in Montréal. That’s also what he was looking to do on his end,” explains Freddy Lloyd.
« Freddy a vraiment ce côté anglophone,: “Freddy really has that anglophone side, whereas I’m more on the French rap side. That’s how Le WarmUp gets solid; it means we complement each other and cover everything,” adds Antony Dagger.
Les deux animateurs ne comptent pas s’ar: The two hosts don’t plan to stop there. They’re working on other projects, including the idea of holding a hip-hop gala in Quebec. Their goal remains the same: to promote Quebec’s hip-hop scene and build a community around the show to get their audience more involved. They also want to remind people that traditional media are no longer an essential platform.
